strengths: Solid theoretical framework: The paper builds rigorously on discrete flow matching with correct derivations of target conditional rates (Proposition 1) and proper extension of projected DFM to variable-length sequences.
Novel approach: Learning sample-dependent insertion/unmasking rates to guide generation order while maintaining terminal distributions addresses a real problem in large action space insertion models.
Efficient training: Single backward pass training using REINFORCE with stop-gradient is technically sound and practically valuable.
Thoughtful parameterization: Kumaraswamy CDFs enable closed-form hazard rates and analytical tractability; the special case interpretation as exponential race is elegant.

Comprehensive experimental analysis: Graph traversal provides interpretable validation; Figure 4 demonstrates learned orders match known optimal structure; thorough ablations on architectural choices.
Clear presentation: Well-organized paper with good figures, comprehensive notation table, and detailed appendix with full proofs.
weaknesses: Training instability requiring constraints: The need to fix b_um=1 significantly undermines the 'learnable' motivation. Figure 6 shows dramatic loss instability with trainable b_um, suggesting fundamental optimization issues rather than a design choice.

Modest empirical improvements: Molecule generation quality improves ~20% relatively (39.5% → 59.2%), but validity gain is only 0.8% absolutely. Improvements vary significantly across configurations, raising questions about consistency.

High sensitivity to hyperparameters: Table 2 shows 59% variation in quality across auxiliary network sizes and nucleus sampling parameters. No principled selection method provided; auxiliary size impact is concerning.
Schedule regularization overhead: Requires careful tuning (tϵ=0.01, δ=0.01) with limited justification, adding complexity and suggesting the base optimization is fragile.

Limited evaluation scope: Only two domains tested; missing comparisons to concurrent methods (EditFlows, ILM); only compares to FlexMDM/MDM, not state-of-the-art; no computational cost analysis despite efficiency claims.
Unexplained dramatic failures: Shared backbone causes 60% performance drop on hard graphs (87.9%→34.2% exact match) with only brief mention; requires better analysis.

Incomplete justification of design choices: Why Kumaraswamy beyond tractability? Why truncation over rescaling? Trade-offs between parameterizations not explored; intuition for when learned orders should differ from uniform missing.

strengths: Technically sound application of projected discrete flow matching with tractable joint training via REINFORCE
Clear empirical validation on graph traversal showing learned locally optimal generation orders with good visualizations
Detailed theoretical development with comprehensive appendix including complete derivations and proofs
Concrete contributions to variable-length generation: enabling learnable target rate schedules without trajectory simulation
weaknesses: Empirical improvements on main task (molecules) are largely confounded by inference parameters (nucleus sampling p), not learned order dynamics; fair comparisons show ~0% improvement

Method requires ad-hoc stabilization rarely highlighted: b_um must be frozen (contradicting 'learnable' dynamics), schedule regularization with arbitrary hyperparameters, undermining robustness claims
Limited experimental scope: only synthetic (ideal structure) and molecule tasks; no text, proteins, or other domains to assess generalization
Fragile joint optimization: shared backbone fails dramatically (34.2% vs 87.9% on hard graphs); significant sensitivity to auxiliary network architecture contradicts tractability claims
Dense presentation obscures core contribution and downplays limitations; key practical constraints (parameter freezing) buried in experiments section rather than highlighted upfront
Missing ablations on parameterization choices, schedule regularization sensitivity, and interpretability of learned schedules; no statistical significance testing
Graph traversal task is artificial best-case scenario with known optimal order; no evidence learning transfers to realistic domains without structured ordering

strengths: Solid technical contribution with sound mathematical framework: Uses projected DFM elegantly to enable joint learning of generator and target rates through learnable Kumaraswamy CDFs
Efficient training procedure: Enables simultaneous optimization of both θ and ϕ parameters using a single backward pass with REINFORCE leave-one-out, avoiding expensive trajectory simulation

Highly convincing graph traversal results: Achieves 88.1% exact match on hard task vs 7.4% for baseline, with analysis showing learned order has correlation −0.91 with optimal order vs −0.09 for FlexMDM
Comprehensive and insightful experimental analysis: Thorough ablations on flexibility vs. stability, clear visualization of learned generation orders, and analysis of diversity-quality tradeoffs
Strong presentation and reproducibility: Well-written with excellent use of figures, comprehensive appendix with complete proofs and derivations, detailed experimental setup
Principled mathematical grounding: All theoretical claims are properly stated as propositions with complete proofs, with proper connection to KL divergence via Proposition 5
weaknesses: Method fragility: Necessity to freeze b_um for training stability (Figure 6) suggests underlying optimization instability. While paper argues this preserves flexibility, the requirement indicates the approach may be inherently constrained

Degenerate solutions and regularization dependency: Need for schedule regularization (Eq. 92) to prevent pathological solutions indicates the loss landscape has problematic properties. Limited sensitivity analysis provided for regularization hyperparameters

Modest practical improvements on real-world tasks: Molecule generation shows only marginal gains (0.9% validity improvement, quality improvements require nucleus sampling tuning). Diversity-quality tradeoff observed with learned order may not be desirable for all applications

Limited experimental scope and domain coverage: Only two main applications tested; graph traversal appears specifically constructed to benefit from order learning (star graphs with known optimal paths). No systematic analysis of when/why order learning helps vs. hurts
Missing baselines and comparisons: No comparison to other order-learning approaches. No wall-clock time comparisons or computational overhead analysis despite adding auxiliary network

Theoretical gaps: Proposition 5 bound on terminal KL may be loose with unknown tightness. Limited analysis of behavior when equilibrium b_um ≠ 1. When does the conditional mixture assumption hold tightly?
